

# Preface {.unnumbered}

Difference-in-differences (DiD) is among the most widely used identification
strategies in empirical economics.  For decades, the two-way fixed effects
(TWFE) regression served as its canonical implementation.  Beginning in the late
2010s, however, a surge of methodological work revealed that TWFE can produce
severely biased — and even sign-reversed — estimates when treatment adoption is
staggered and effects are heterogeneous.  These notes document the resulting
"new DiD" literature: its theoretical foundations, its failure modes, and the
modern estimators developed in response.

## Structure

- **Part I — Introduction.**
  The canonical $2 \times 2$ setup, the potential outcomes framework and ATT,
  and TWFE as a multi-period generalisation.  The closing section surveys the
  recent methodological debates that motivate the remainder of the notes.

- **Part II — Identification Assumptions.**
  The core of DiD identification is the parallel trends assumption (PTA).
  @roth2022 showed that the common practice of conditioning on a passed
  pre-trend test distorts the sampling distribution of post-treatment estimates,
  producing size distortions and reduced power.  When the PTA is plausible only
  after conditioning on observables, @abadie2005 proposed an IPW-DiD estimator,
  and @santanna2020 extended this to a doubly robust (DR-DiD) procedure; for
  high-dimensional covariates, @chernozhukov2018 developed double/debiased
  machine learning (DML), adapted to the DiD setting by @chang2020.  When
  unobserved time-varying shocks threaten the PTA entirely, @arkhangelsky2021
  combined synthetic control weights with DiD (SDID), and @rambachan2023
  proposed honest sensitivity analysis that bounds inference under partial
  violations of parallel trends.  The part also covers partial compliance:
  @imbens1994 established the LATE framework, and @chaisemartin2015 extended
  it to fuzzy DiD via the Wald-DiD estimator.

- **Part III — Staggered Adoption.**
  @goodman2021 showed that under staggered treatment timing the TWFE coefficient
  is a variance-weighted average of all possible $2 \times 2$ sub-comparisons —
  some of which carry negative weights, because already-treated units are used as
  implicit controls for later-treated units.  This diagnosis sparked a wave of
  robust estimators: @callaway2021 proposed group-time ATTs using never- or
  not-yet-treated units as clean controls; @borusyak2024 developed an imputation
  approach that fits TWFE only on untreated observations; @sun2021 proposed an
  interaction-weighted estimator for heterogeneity-robust event studies;
  @chaisemartin2020 derived a robust estimator accommodating treatment switching;
  and @roth2023 derived the semiparametrically efficient estimator for staggered
  rollout designs, nesting the above approaches while supporting both
  $t$-based and permutation inference.

- **Part IV — Heterogeneous Effects and Extensions.**
  @athey2006 departed from the additive error structure underlying standard DiD
  and proposed the changes-in-changes (CiC) model, which identifies the full
  counterfactual distribution under non-separable unobservables.  For
  non-negative, binary, or fractional outcomes, @wooldridge2023 showed how
  pooled quasi-MLE within the linear exponential family circumvents the incidental
  parameters problem in staggered designs.  @callaway2024 demonstrated that naive
  continuous-treatment TWFE suffers from analogous negative-weight problems and
  proposed causal dose-response functions under generalised parallel trends.  The
  part also covers triple-differences (DDD) and quantile DiD.

## Audience

These notes assume familiarity with linear regression, panel data methods, and
the potential outcomes framework, at the level of a first-year graduate course
in econometrics
